chapters.title: Chapter 7: The Wrong Kind of Fun
Chapter 8: The Chair He Never Sat In
Chapter 14: I Trust You to Bring Me Home
Chapter 19: The Gear in the Cloud

spans.text: The team had been on Sky Islands for one breath, and Pip Pop was already in the air.

He had not planned to be. He had planned, very seriously, on the walk through the portal, to scout before he announced and to wait before he moved. He had repeated the plan to himself the way you repeat a song you do not want to forget. Then his boots touched the floating grass, the sign over the platform read FALLING RESET ENABLED in clean white letters, and his whole round face went up with the words.
Captain,
he said.
Captain. The sign.
I see it.
It says FALLING RESET ENABLED.
It does.
That is the best sign I have ever read in any world ever built.
You have not read very many signs, Pip.
That is also true, and it is still the best one.

The letters slid a half square left, a quarter back, then settled where they had started. The slide had a shape. The shape was wind. Pip did not know that yet. He knew the letters were good letters and the grass was good grass and somewhere off the edge there were balloons, and a place with balloons and a falling-is-fine sign was, by every measurement his small pink body could take, the greatest place ever made.
The air smelled like the five minutes before a summer storm. Not a warning. A quality. Sky-air doing sky-air things.
I live here now,
he announced.

His voice came out higher than he meant. He had not meant to announce anything. Announcements went after the scout. Captain had said so in three worlds. Scout first, announce after. Pip had heard the rule. He had even said it in his head on the way in. But the sign was bright and the morning was big and one announcement could not cost anyone a thing.

This was the part Pip did not understand yet, the part the sky was about to teach him with great patience and no cruelty. His feet were a separate country with their own government, and they had bounced him through fourteen years of worlds before his head could vote, and every time the bounce had been a joke and the joke had been the point, and no one had ever shown him the bill until the bill came due in the middle of the sky.
The bill was not due this morning. This morning the feet only leaned.

They leaned toward a blue fan pad set into the grass, a small painted arrow on it pointing straight up. The fan pad was a good color. The fan pad was waiting. His feet leaned, and his head, which was supposed to be in charge, watched the feet lean and tried to recall whether it had approved the motion.
Together,
spans.speaker: Captain

spans.text: Captain said,
can include enthusiastic previews. It does not include solo launches.
spans.speaker: Captain

spans.text: Captain Cubemelon's lens, the small blue cyber goggle on the left of his cube head, turned a half-tick. A full click meant worried. A half-tick meant paying attention. Pip had spent a lot of time learning the difference. He rocked his weight back onto his heels. Still ready. A little less ready.

In Captain's other hand, the Gravity Wrench hummed against his palm, low and even, the way it had hummed since Green Hills Lab. The hum did not float off the way the rest of the morning seemed to want to. It stayed down. It held the ground steady under Captain even where there was barely ground.
A small white cloud drifted down toward them. Two dot eyes. A half-circle mouth. It moved with the air, not against it.
Welcome to Sky Islands,
the cloud said.
I am Cloudle. Please enjoy your visit. Please anchor your save. Please do not confuse safe falling with useful falling.
Falling,
spans.speaker: Pip

spans.text: Pip said.
She said falling.
spans.speaker: Pip

spans.text: She said three pleases,
spans.speaker: Drip

spans.text: Drip said.
Pip. Three of them.
spans.speaker: Drip

spans.text: I heard falling.
You heard one word out of the third please.
Was it the important word?
That is what we are about to find out.

Cloudle did not repeat the warning. Clouds who repeat polite warnings only teach builders to stop hearing them. The other words drifted out the back of Pip's head, and only falling stuck, the way a burr sticks to a sock.
Then the wind lifted him off his feet.

Not a strong wind. A polite one. Sky Islands gusts were almost always polite the first time, the way a host is polite before deciding what kind of visitor you are. This gust decided Pip was the kind who wanted a ride. It slid under his pink suit, found the place where his small body curved away from the grass, and lifted him with neat, practiced efficiency.

The efficiency surprised him. The gust did not lift him sideways or forward. It got under his center and went straight up, the way something does when it has done the job a long time. He spun once, twice, three times. He waved at the team. The wave was already a habit, the part of him that remembered everyone even when the rest of him forgot to remember anything. The wave went out, and he vanished below the edge of the island with a long bright
"Wheeeee."
A blink later he popped back onto the start pad.

Not a thud. Not a click. The pop was the sound of a small pink body set back exactly where it belonged by a system that knew exactly where that was. The grass did not bend. His suit did not ripple. He was simply where he had been, plus three seconds of being somewhere else.
Again,
he whispered.

He whispered it the way you whisper a wish you do not quite expect to be granted. His pink hands were already lifting toward the fan pad. His feet had not received the news that the trip had been a problem. His feet had received different news entirely, which was that the trip had been wonderful.
Moss Guard had not moved.

He stood at the edge with one large hand flat on the grass before he leaned to look over it. The hand was a brace. He braced before he looked, because bracing first was the whole difference between a careful look and a long fall. He had taught the habit to himself a long time ago, before there were teammates to teach it to. Habits stayed around longer than the situations that built them.
Far below, the clouds spread soft and endless and nowhere near close enough to land on.
No one lives over an edge until we understand the edge,
spans.speaker: Moss

spans.text: Moss said.
That is what makes it an edge,
spans.speaker: Pip

spans.text: Pip said, and his feet leaned again.

This time Captain caught him. The grip closed on the small fabric loop sewn into the back of Pip's suit, firm enough to hold, gentle enough not to bruise. Captain had been catching small bouncers all day, all week, across all the worlds, until catching had become a skill he sometimes wished he had less use for. The loop had been earned the hard way, the first night in Green Hills Lab, when Captain had scrabbled for somewhere to grab and found nothing.
We test together,
spans.speaker: Captain

spans.text: Captain said.
I know,
spans.speaker: Pip

spans.text: Pip said.
I am working on it.
spans.speaker: Pip

spans.text: That is good.
spans.speaker: Captain

spans.text: Drip crouched by the open toolbox at the team's feet. He had meant to scan the wind. The toolbox lid was up from when Patch had been hunting earlier, and Drip's eye went down into it the way other people's eyes went to a watch. Drip counted tools the way other people counted seconds.

He started to file the breeze's texture, then stopped himself. Frost Cave had taught him that filing first was sometimes a habit and not a help. He looked at the team. Fine. He looked at the world. The world was the world. He let it be both before he let himself look back into the box.

Brick already had her sketchpad out. She mixed a color in her head and did not paint it yet. Anchored green. She tucked the name into the corner of her notebook in her smallest hand, a curl on the f, a hook on the p, the writing only the island was meant to read.
Forty islands,
spans.speaker: Patch

spans.text: Patch said. He had his measuring tool in his hand, the one with the worn handle and the small notch he had filed into the side on his second day. Patch collected measuring tools the way Pip collected bounces. His head measured things even when his hands were still.
Forty?
spans.speaker: Drip

spans.text: Drip looked up.
That I can count from here. Probably more.
Some of them are not actually there,
spans.speaker: Brick

spans.text: Brick said.
She had seen it first. Painters notice when a thing is not quite present. She pointed at an island in the middle distance, a green shape that did not hold still in the eye.
That one is not stable. It comes and goes.
In what pattern?
spans.speaker: Drip

spans.text: Drip asked.
Roughly every six seconds.
Drip's tablet beeped on its own. The tablet, calibrated in Frost Cave to listen before it scanned, had noticed too. It put a small label on the wavering island. AS-IF.
As-if islands,
spans.speaker: Drip

spans.text: Drip said.
That is what the tablet calls them. As if they are there. Partly real. Partly draft.
spans.speaker: Drip

spans.text: How many?
spans.speaker: Captain

spans.text: Captain asked.
Drip scanned the sky. The scan came back busy. He held the number a moment, the way you hold a number you do not love.
About half of what we can see flickers.
Half of Sky Islands is draft.
Roughly.

Captain's lens clicked one full notch, into worried, then eased back to the half-tick. He had spent half a day in a draft scene once. He did not want to spend another. He filed the worry where Pip could not see it and kept his voice level.

Pip heard the part where Moss had said no one lives over an edge, and the part where the tablet said half the world was a draft, and a small new thing happened in his chest. The word falling, which had always been the fun word, the word for the part of bouncing where you rode the air for a second before landing, turned over in him and showed a different side. Falling, all by itself, with no landing attached, was a longer word. It went on. It did not end at the grass.

He did not have anywhere to put that, so he tucked it into the small inside pocket of his suit, the one where he kept his bounce-toy, the one where the day's noticings went. The pocket felt a little heavier with the word in it. He would find it later.
He turned away from the fan pad.

It cost him something to do it. The fan pad was blue and the arrow pointed up and the whole machine of it was practically begging. He turned anyway. He took one careful step backward. He set his pink hands behind his back, which was the small dull lever his head had lately learned to pull, and his feet, outvoted for once, settled flat on the grass.

The grass held him. He held the grass. It was the smallest agreement on Sky Islands, and he was, for the first time in fourteen years of bouncing, one half of it instead of a thing the world had to keep catching.

He kept his other hand in the pocket, near the bounce-toy without taking it out. The bounce-toy was the size of a marble and it bounced against his palm where no one could see, and that was the whole trick of it: a bounce that did not leave the ground, a fun that did not cost the team a thing. One pink stripe, one white stripe, a small scratch from a hard patience-moment in Sand Canyon. He did not squeeze it. He only knew it was there. Knowing it was there helped.

The wind came again. Three steady, then a gust, then three steady. He felt it on the back of his neck where his suit ended, and he noticed it came from the same direction as the first one. He had no tablet to log it. So he tucked the noticing in beside the falling word. The pocket was getting busy.

The gust had a personality. Polite the first time, less polite the second, exactly the same on the third. It did not change with how he reacted to it. It came when it came. It did not care about him. He had never once been treated as not-the-center before, and he turned the feeling over, and it did not feel bad. It felt true.
Pip,
spans.speaker: Captain

spans.text: Captain said.
Yes.
You are standing very still.
I am working on it.
That is good.
Is it?
It is.

Pip tried not to feel proud about standing still. Pride about standing still was a sneaky feeling. It made standing still feel like a thing you had finished, which made you want to stop. Pride was an enemy of patience. He had not known that this morning. He knew it now.
He turned away from the fan pad. He set his pink hands behind his back. He waited.
He was very bad at waiting.
